text.p: Specialist footcare and footwear group Scholl Plc said on Tuesday that its reorganisation plans were "going well," and predicted a satisfactory outcome for 1997.

In a telephone interview with Reuters, chairman Stuart Wallis said the goal of the reorganisation had been to "concentrate on the core business, which is the Scholl brand, and remove ourselves from extraneous businesses which have not yielded the sort of profits we were looking for."

The shake-up led to an exceptional charge of 35.7 million stg against group earnings, pushing Scholl into the red with a pre-tax loss of 15.12 million stg compared with a profit of 18.1 million a year before. Underlying profits rose 13.8 percent to 20.6 million stg.
Wallis said the group had taken all the charges it needed and was now in a position to concentrate on expanding its business, particularly in eastern Europe and Asia Pacific.
The company sold a number of non-core activities during the year, including a British herbal remedies brand and two French operations.

With the acquisition of the South American Scholl business in February, Wallis said Scholl now owned the brand name throughout the world, with the exception of the U.S, where it belongs to Schering Plough Corp.
He said the two companies had greatly improved relations and were cooperating on marketing a number of products.

In retail, Scholl reduced the number of shops to around 100 from 150 two years ago, leaving 70 in Britain, 14 in Scandinavia and 12 in Spain. Some 33 shops were sold last year, with the company getting out of the Canadian market altogether. It also disposed of 11 stores in Germany. Scholl said that on a like-for-like basis sales at its stores rose seven percent in 1996.

Wallis said the group planned to expand organically and through selective acquisitions. He said Hungary and Poland showed strong growth last year, adding "we see further growth opportunities both there and in the rest of Eastern Europe."
